architecture.ai_summary:
Liza Pairing Empowered On-rails. Liza is a Go-based collaboration control plane for disciplined human-agent pairing and peer-supervised multi-agent software delivery. Its product is a controlled, auditable delivery workflow rather than a thin model launcher: behavioral contracts require agents to externalize intent, assumptions, evidence, and decisions, while deterministic orchestration enforces ownership, lifecycle, review, and integration rules. Pairing and multi-agent modes share the same reliability invariants but assign gates differently—the human holds them during pairing, while persisted checkpoints and independent peers hold them during autonomous execution. This separation preserves judgment as an agent responsibility without granting agents unilateral authority over durable project state.

In multi-agent operation, an approved goal or committed specification becomes declarative pipeline work. Supervisors select and claim eligible tasks before invoking a configured provider, establish generation-fenced lease ownership, prepare isolated Git worktrees, and construct role-specific prompts from durable specifications and coordination state. Doers implement and submit committed candidates; independent reviewers inspect the applicable review boundary, validate acceptance evidence, and issue binding verdicts under configurable quorum and provider-diversity policies. Approved work advances toward the integration branch through serialized, guarded Git operations that detect drift or conflicting ref updates. A file-backed blackboard records current tasks, agents, sprint state, leases, histories, diagnostics, and approvals, while append-only logs, alerts, and the terminal interface expose the same authoritative workflow rather than creating parallel control paths.

The architecture deliberately separates judgment, policy, durable facts, and side effects. Agents interpret requirements, plan, implement, and review; the deterministic control plane owns state mutation, task eligibility, lease recovery, generation authority, worktree readiness, dependency ordering, review progression, and merge coordination. User-facing commands validate and translate requests but delegate lifecycle decisions to authoritative operations. Persisted models define the shared vocabulary, declarative pipeline configuration defines roles, role-pair states, transitions, timeouts, context requirements, and review policy, and candidate-state validation rejects illegal schemas, dependencies, artifact references, sprint relationships, authorities, or transitions before they become durable. Provider invocation, Git and process control, filesystem paths, terminal presentation, and repository-index integrations remain boundary concerns so workflow policy neither leaks into prompts nor becomes coupled to one model, operating system, or target-project toolchain.

Load-bearing constraints include atomic locked blackboard updates, attributable mutations, supervisor-assigned ownership, renewable leases with stale-generation fencing, isolated worktrees, committed and reviewable candidates, independent review, and completion evidence that corresponds to the current integration state. Behavioral code is expected to encode specification intent in tests before implementation unless a documented waiver applies; validation must exercise observable outcomes rather than merely report green commands. Bounded retries, anomaly detection, circuit-breaker responses, and structured handoff prevent failed agents or review loops from consuming work indefinitely. Secret masking and state hygiene constrain what may enter prompts, streams, logs, diagnostics, and retained records. Optional semantic, repository-map, symbol, and functional-cluster indexes improve orientation only: source files, Git state, validation results, and persisted workflow state remain authoritative.

New behavior belongs at the narrowest boundary that owns its invariant. Command syntax, access checks, and presentation stay at the CLI edge; durable lifecycle changes receive one authoritative mutation path; new shared facts enter the domain model; role or transition policy enters declarative pipeline configuration; and rules spanning tasks, agents, dependencies, artifacts, reviews, or sprints enter candidate-state validation. Provider-specific launch mechanics and optional navigation tooling remain adapters, while project commands and paths must come from configuration or detection so runtime behavior remains stack-agnostic. Changes to contracts or prompts belong in their repository masters and must flow through the branded embedded-artifact regeneration path, preventing installed copies from drifting. Tests should emphasize observable lifecycle outcomes and the failure boundaries most exposed to regression: invalid-transition rejection, concurrent mutation, lease expiry, stale generations, resubmission, reviewer quorum, dependency repair, integration drift, and merge safety.
